questions.prompt: Oxidation in electron-transfer terms is…
options: gain of neutrons in every reaction.
questions.explanation: Oxidation means electron loss.

questions.prompt: Reduction in electron-transfer terms is…
questions.explanation: Reduction means electron gain.

questions.prompt: In Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, zinc is…
questions.explanation: Zinc loses two electrons.

questions.prompt: In Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, the copper ion is…
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons to form neutral copper.

questions.prompt: What does an oxidising agent do?
options: Accepts electrons and is itself reduced
Donates electrons and is itself reduced
questions.explanation: It causes another species to lose electrons by accepting them.

questions.prompt: What does a reducing agent do?
options: Accepts electrons and is itself oxidised
Donates electrons and is itself oxidised
questions.explanation: It supplies the electrons gained by the reduced species.

questions.prompt: In Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is…
questions.explanation: Magnesium donates electrons and is oxidised.

questions.prompt: In the same Mg / Cu²⁺ reaction, the oxidising agent is…
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ accepts electrons and is reduced.

questions.prompt: Which oxidation-state change represents oxidation?
questions.explanation: An increase in oxidation state is oxidation.

questions.prompt: Why must oxidation and reduction be paired in a complete redox process?
options: Electrons are created without a source.
Electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
Both species must gain all electrons.
questions.explanation: Overall electron and charge conservation requires matched loss and gain.

questions.prompt: Which is a balanced oxidation half-equation for magnesium?
questions.explanation: Atoms and charge balance: 0 = +2 − 2.

questions.prompt: Which is a balanced reduction half-equation for Cu²⁺?
questions.explanation: Two electrons neutralise the +2 charge.

questions.prompt: Which is a balanced oxidation half-equation for bromide?
questions.explanation: Two bromide ions form one Br₂ molecule and release two electrons.

questions.prompt: Which half-equation produces aluminium metal?
questions.explanation: Three electrons are needed per Al³⁺ ion.

questions.prompt: What is the oxidation state of a pure element such as Cu(s)?
questions.explanation: An element in its uncombined form has oxidation state zero.

questions.prompt: What is the oxidation state of iron in Fe₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Three O atoms contribute −6; two Fe atoms must total +6.

questions.prompt: What is the oxidation state of carbon in CO₂?
questions.explanation: Two oxygens contribute −4, so carbon is +4.

questions.prompt: What is the oxidation state of carbon in CO?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is −2 here, so carbon is +2.

questions.prompt: How many electrons must 2Al atoms lose when they become 2Al³⁺?
questions.explanation: Each Al loses three electrons; two lose six.

questions.prompt: What must be balanced in a half-equation?
questions.explanation: Electrons are included to balance charge while preserving atoms.

questions.prompt: What carries charge through an electrolyte?
options: Electrons travelling freely through the liquid like in a wire
questions.explanation: Positive and negative ions move through the electrolyte.

questions.prompt: What carries charge through the external metal wires?
questions.explanation: Metallic wires conduct through mobile electrons.

questions.prompt: In an electrolytic cell, cations migrate towards the…
options: salt bridge only in every setup.
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract; cations move towards the negative electrode.

questions.prompt: In an electrolytic cell, anions migrate towards the…
options: battery casing instead of the electrolyte.
questions.explanation: Negative ions move towards the positive electrode.

questions.prompt: At which electrode does reduction always occur?
options: Both electrodes are always oxidation sites only
questions.explanation: Cathode names the electrode where reduction occurs.

questions.prompt: At which electrode does oxidation always occur?
questions.explanation: Anode names the electrode where oxidation occurs.

questions.prompt: Why can a molten ionic compound conduct while its solid may not?
options: The melt always becomes a metal.
Melting frees the ions to move.
questions.explanation: Ion mobility changes; the solid already contains ions but they are fixed in the lattice.

questions.prompt: What drives a non-spontaneous electrolytic reaction?
options: A catalyst that supplies unlimited electrons without a circuit
questions.explanation: Electrical energy drives the electrode reactions.

questions.prompt: Is “cathode is negative” a universal rule for every electrochemical cell type?
options: No; cathode always means reduction, while polarity depends on cell type.
Yes; every galvanic cathode is negative too.
questions.explanation: Electrolytic cathodes are negative; galvanic cathodes are positive.

questions.prompt: Which distinction is correct?
options: Ion migration means ions become neutral halfway through the solution automatically.
Ion migration moves ions through solution; discharge transfers electrons at an electrode.
Discharge is the same as filtering.
Electrons carry all electrolyte current without any ions.
questions.explanation: Transport and electrode reaction are related but different processes.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what metal forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten NaCl?
questions.explanation: Molten NaCl contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻, with no water competing.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what forms at the anode during electrolysis of molten NaCl?
questions.explanation: Molten NaCl contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻, with no water competing.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what metal forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten PbBr₂?
questions.explanation: Pb²⁺ is reduced; bromide is oxidised to Br₂.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what forms at the anode during electrolysis of molten PbBr₂?
questions.explanation: Pb²⁺ is reduced; bromide is oxidised to Br₂.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what metal forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten MgCl₂?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ gains electrons; chloride loses electrons.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what forms at the anode during electrolysis of molten MgCl₂?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ gains electrons; chloride loses electrons.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what metal forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten CaBr₂?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ is reduced and bromide forms Br₂.

questions.prompt: With inert electrodes, what forms at the anode during electrolysis of molten CaBr₂?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ is reduced and bromide forms Br₂.

questions.prompt: Why is sodium obtained at the cathode of molten NaCl rather than hydrogen?
options: Sodium is a gas at all temperatures.
The cathode is an oxidation site.
There is no water in the molten salt to compete.
Chloride gains the electrons to make sodium.
questions.explanation: Molten-salt and aqueous product rules differ because their available species differ.

questions.prompt: In molten lead(II) bromide, which pair of half-equations is correct?
questions.explanation: Lead ions are reduced and bromide ions oxidised with two electrons balanced.

questions.prompt: What normally forms at the cathode in aqueous CuSO₄ with inert electrodes?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ can be reduced to copper under this usual aqueous comparison.

questions.prompt: What normally forms at the inert anode in aqueous CuSO₄?
questions.explanation: Water is oxidised; sulfate is not normally discharged in this school comparison.

questions.prompt: With copper electrodes in CuSO₄, what happens at the anode?
options: Copper plates out at the anode.
questions.explanation: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ is anode oxidation.

questions.prompt: Why can Cu²⁺ concentration remain approximately constant with copper electrodes?
options: Every sulfate ion becomes a copper ion.
Copper ions are replenished at the dissolving anode as they are removed at the cathode.
questions.explanation: Ideal transfer balances copper dissolution and deposition.

questions.prompt: What cathode gas is expected from ordinary concentrated aqueous NaCl with inert electrodes?
questions.explanation: Water is reduced in preference to Na⁺ under the ordinary aqueous conditions.

questions.prompt: What anode gas is usually produced from concentrated brine with inert electrodes?
questions.explanation: High chloride concentration supports chlorine evolution; conditions matter.

questions.prompt: What products are expected for concentrated aqueous CuCl₂ with inert electrodes in the stated model?
options: Copper at the anode and sodium at the cathode
Copper at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ is reduced; chloride can be oxidised at a suitable inert anode.

questions.prompt: Which information matters when predicting aqueous electrolysis products?
options: Only the solution volume, regardless of species
Only alphabetical order of ion names
Ion concentrations, electrode materials and conditions
questions.explanation: Water competition and electrode kinetics make conditions important.

questions.prompt: Which equation gives hydrogen from water at an alkaline cathode?
questions.explanation: Reduction of water produces hydrogen and hydroxide ions.

questions.prompt: Why is “all anions in water discharge equally easily” incorrect?
options: Every anion is a neutral atom.
Some anions remain spectators while water or another species is oxidised.
Anions always move to the cathode in electrolysis.
Water cannot ever react at an electrode.
questions.explanation: Product selection is not determined by migration alone.

questions.prompt: What is the H₂:O₂ volume ratio from acidified-water electrolysis at equal temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ gives twice as many moles of hydrogen.

questions.prompt: Which electrode produces H₂ in acidified-water electrolysis?
questions.explanation: H⁺ or water is reduced at the cathode.

questions.prompt: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
questions.explanation: A glowing-splint test identifies oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which gas gives the characteristic pop with a burning splint?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns rapidly when mixed with oxygen from air.

questions.prompt: Why use a suitable electrolyte rather than relying on very pure water alone?
options: It changes oxygen atoms into hydrogen atoms.
It removes the need for electrodes.
It provides enough mobile ions for useful conduction.
It guarantees chloride-free water gives chlorine.
questions.explanation: Very pure water is a poor conductor because its ion concentration is very low.

questions.prompt: Acidified-water electrolysis gives 5 mL of O₂. At the same temperature and pressure, what H₂ volume is predicted in mL?
questions.explanation: The mole and volume ratio H₂:O₂ is 2:1.

questions.prompt: Acidified-water electrolysis gives 12 mL of O₂. At the same temperature and pressure, what H₂ volume is predicted in mL?
questions.explanation: The mole and volume ratio H₂:O₂ is 2:1.

questions.prompt: Acidified-water electrolysis gives 25 mL of O₂. At the same temperature and pressure, what H₂ volume is predicted in mL?
questions.explanation: The mole and volume ratio H₂:O₂ is 2:1.

questions.prompt: An ideal water electrolysis gives 18 mL of H₂ and 9 mL of O₂. What is the total gas volume in mL at the same conditions?
questions.explanation: Add the two volumes measured at the same conditions: 18 + 9 = 27 mL.

questions.prompt: At 100% efficiency, 2 mol of electrons pass through an acidified-water cathode. How many moles of H₂ form?
questions.explanation: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ requires 2 mol e⁻ per mole of hydrogen.

questions.prompt: What is dissolved in molten cryolite for aluminium extraction?
questions.explanation: Alumina supplies the aluminium-containing ions.

questions.prompt: What is an important function of cryolite?
options: It lowers the operating temperature relative to pure alumina.
It provides all the aluminium atoms instead of alumina.
questions.explanation: Cryolite forms a conducting molten mixture at a lower temperature than pure alumina would require.

questions.prompt: Where is aluminium metal formed?
options: In the external copper wire only
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ gains electrons at the cathode.

questions.prompt: Why are carbon anodes consumed?
options: The anodes are reduced to sodium.
Aluminium deposits consume them mechanically only.
Carbon reacts to form carbon oxides.
questions.explanation: Oxidation at the carbon anode leads mainly to CO₂ in the ideal model, with real variations.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct overall ideal carbon-anode equation?
questions.explanation: The balanced equation conserves Al, O and C for a CO₂-only anode model.

questions.prompt: Which is the net carbon-anode half-equation in the CO₂ model?
questions.explanation: Oxide ions and carbon produce CO₂ while four electrons are released.

questions.prompt: Why is the molten state essential in this cell?
options: Every solid ionic compound conducts equally well.
The electrolyte ions must be mobile.
Molten means there are no ions.
questions.explanation: Ion movement carries current through the electrolyte.

questions.prompt: What does assuming 100% current efficiency mean in the mass model?
options: The electrical supply needs no energy.
All industrial cells have no losses.
All passed charge produces the specified electrode reaction.
questions.explanation: It is an idealisation; side reactions and inefficiencies can reduce actual yield.

questions.prompt: How many moles of electrons are required to form 1 mol of Al from Al³⁺?
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.

questions.prompt: At 100% efficiency, 6 mol of electrons reduce Al³⁺. Using 27 g/mol, what mass of Al forms in grams?
In silver-halide photography, what forms the dark developed image?
questions.explanation: Development reduces silver ions to visible silver metal.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the developing agent?
options: It supplies new silver nuclei from carbon.
It oxidises all silver metal to erase the image.
It reduces exposed silver-halide grains and is itself oxidised.
questions.explanation: The developer supplies reducing action that amplifies the latent image.

questions.prompt: What does photographic fixer remove?
options: All the developed metallic silver in a normal successful process
Every atom of the support film
questions.explanation: Fixing removes light-sensitive unexposed material and stabilises the image.

questions.prompt: Why is the first photographic image called a negative?
options: More-exposed regions develop darker while masked regions remain lighter.
Every ion on it has negative charge.
questions.explanation: The light–dark relationship is reversed relative to the original subject.

questions.prompt: Which half-equation represents silver-image formation during development?
questions.explanation: Silver ions gain electrons, so the process is reduction.

questions.prompt: What metal removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide in thermite?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is sufficiently reactive to reduce the iron oxide in this comparison.

questions.prompt: Which equation is balanced for thermite?
questions.explanation: Two Al and two Fe atoms balance, along with three O atoms.

questions.prompt: Which species is oxidised in thermite?
questions.explanation: Al goes from 0 to +3, while Fe goes from +3 to 0.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are transferred in 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe?
questions.explanation: Two Al atoms each lose three electrons, matching reduction of two Fe³⁺ centres.

questions.prompt: Why does copper not replace aluminium in the same iron-oxide thermite comparison?
options: Copper is more reactive than every metal.
Copper is less reactive than iron in this comparison.
questions.explanation: A less reactive metal cannot perform the same oxygen-removal role under the stated conditions.
